newsitem.title: UK: Reed plays down U.S. court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Reed plays down U.S. court ruling.

text.p: Anglo-Dutch publishing group Reed Elsevier on Thursday played down a U.S. court ruling which threatened to undermine its Lexis-Nexis unit and cut prices in the multi-million dollar business of running legal databases.
Reports of the ruling, along with a downgrade on Reed shares by a major brokerage, sent Reed Elsevier shares sharply lower on Thursday.
The stock closed down 17p or 2.7 percent at 608-1/2, the biggest decliner in the FTSE 100 index, in heavy trade of more than 11 million shares.

The U.S. court ruling removed a copyright claimed by a company called West Publishing, bought by Canadian publishing giant Thomson last year for $1.4 billion, to publish the text of U.S. court decisions.
The ruling -- which Thomson said it would appeal -- meant that rival publishers can copy decisions in West law books into their computers and then issue them in book or electronic form.
A report in the New York Times said the ruling was expected to drive down the price of legal research in the United States.
But Reed said the judgement would have a "minimal" impact on Lexis-Nexis, which it bought in 1994 for $1.5 billion.
"The value that large legal publishers like Lexis-Nexis offer the legal community extends far beyond the text of legal decisions," the company said in a statement.

"The breadth and depth of the legal information offerings, the editorial enhancements and the search and navigation systems...are the foundation of Lexis-Nexis, which is unaffected by the recent West decision," it said.

Traders and analysts said the U.S. court ruling dented confidence in Reed, which has invested heavily in expanding its on-line activities in recent years, though it should have little real impact on profits in the foreseeable future.
Merrill analyst Meg Geldens confirmed she had cut her short-term rating on Reed shares to "accumulate" from "buy," but said the move was not directly related to the West court decision.
Rather, it reflected the rally in Reed shares in recent weeks, which carried the stock to a record 633p earlier in May.
"The price seemed a little rich," Geldens said, "but that is very much short-term, it is an excellent company with a lot of proprietary content."
Geldens agreed that the U.S. court ruling was not a major threat to Lexis, estimated to deliver about seven percent of Reed Elsevier group profits.
"Lexis and West have a very strong franchise," she said, "it is going to be very difficult for someone to replicate the online services that these guys have been running for years."
